# Using large language models to create lexicons for interpretable text models with high content validity: the Suicide Risk Lexicon

**Authors:** Daniel M. Low; Osiris Rankin; Daniel D. L. Coppersmith; Kate H. Bentley; Matthew K. Nock; Satrajit S. Ghosh

**Affiliations:** 1DAIR Center, Child Mind Institute, New York, NY, USA | 2Department of Psychology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA | 3Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, MA, USA | 4Spring Health, USA | 5Department of Psychiatry, Mass General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 6Department of Epidemiology, Harvard Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 7Boston Children’s Hospital/Franciscan Children’s, Boston, MA, USA | 8MIT McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Cambridge, MA, USA | 9Department of Otolaryngology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Researchers often want to measure a variety of constructs such as anxiety, discrimination, or loneliness in text data from surveys, interviews, social media, and electronic health records. Using large language models (LLMs) –while optimal for text classification– remain infeasible for some researchers due to concerns around computational expertise, cost, privacy, and compute requirements. Therefore, some researchers prefer to use lightweight models for large datasets or interpretable models to avoid mistakes in high-stakes scenarios such as suicide risk detection. Lexicons offer simple baselines to LLMs by searching for relevant phrases –and can be used together with LLMs to guarantee capturing specific keywords in a deterministic way. However, building new lexicons is resource intensive. In this study, we found that GPT-4 turbo was able to automatically create a lexicon for 49 known risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors, which we release as the Suicide Risk Lexicon. Generating a lexicon with LLMs quickly measures most constructs relevant for suicide risk detection, resulting in high content validity. This lexicon was able to accurately predict risk in crisis counseling conversations. After validating the lexicon with clinician ratings, the lexicon modestly outperformed the LIWC lexicon –which has low content validity for mental illness– and performed similarly to some black-box deep learning models. Due to using an interpretable approach with high content validity, we discovered that active suicidal ideation and direct self-injury were stronger indicators of imminent risk than passive suicidal ideation and depressed mood in this ecological setting (i.e., naturalistic counseling conversations as the crisis is happening, as opposed to assessments or interviews about retrospective symptoms). To simplify creating new lexicons for other research domains, we introduce a Python package, construct-tracker, that works with a variety of LLMs. In sum, while we recommend using LLMs for text classification, they remain out of reach for many researchers. Our work demonstrates that LLMs –despite being black-boxes– can counterintuitively create interpretable models by generating lexicons, when this is preferred. However, more studies are needed to test how these methods generalize to other datasets and psychological domains. Furthermore, we highlight the broader application of lexicons beyond measurement, including their use in benchmarking LLM performance.

## Abstract

Researchers studying mental health often want to measure specific constructs –such as hopelessness, loneliness, or financial concerns– in text from social media, therapy transcripts, or crisis counseling conversations. Using a suicide risk detection as a use case, this study used a large language model to automatically generate a list of words and phrases associated with 49 known risk factors for suicide risk, which we call the Suicide Risk Lexicon. This lexicon allowed researchers to build a simple, interpretable model that predicted imminent suicide risk in crisis counseling conversations while also revealing which risk factors —such as mentions of lethal means and active suicidal plans— mattered most.

## Introduction

Text data are ubiquitous: from text messages and social media posts to legal documents and electronic health records. A frequent goal in analyzing text is to quantify the presence and degree of different constructs. Examples of use cases include identifying electronic health records that mention certain causes of symptoms, finding cases of text messages where threats happened, tracking mentions in sleep issues from psychotherapy transcripts, quantifying the presence of abortion-related debates in political discourse, and many others. The most commonly used methods for text classification methods include lexicons and deep learning including large language models. A lexicon or dictionary is a list of tokens (words and phrases) that can be used to measure constructs in a text document, by counting token matches for those constructs (Boyd, Ashokkumar, Seraj, & Pennebaker, 2022a; Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010).

Deep learning methods including LLMs have certain advantages over lexicons for text classification (e.g., see (Lin & Morency, 2023; Schwartz et al., 2013)) since they can learn: contextual information such as hedges, degree modifiers, and modality (e.g., differences between “I sort of feel sad”, “I think I feel sad”, “I really feel sad”, “I can’t help feeling sad” or differences between “I barely eat”, “I might not eat”, “I can’t seem to eat”, “I must not eat”); word sense ambiguity (e.g., “feeling blue” vs. “blue chair”); cardinal or ordinal intensity of a construct (e.g., sadness intensity is 0.7 out of 1) whereas lexicons perform binary detection (e.g., sadness is present if its tokens appear); slight variations on tokens such as morphological derivations, slang, creative neologisms, and spelling errors in target documents, which could result in false negatives with lexicons; and certain linguistic information (e.g., indices of sentence complexity) that may help map text patterns to some target variable in a data-driven way. Therefore, when conditions for using LLMs are viable, LLMs are generally preferred to lexicons to optimize predictive performance.

That said, it is important to stress that different NLP methods can complement each other: they can strengthen conclusions when results converge, reveal different properties of the target phenomena, or potentially unveil limitations and trade-offs of the different methods when results diverge (for systematic comparisons, see Eijsbroek et al. (2025); D. M. Low, Mair, Nock, and Ghosh (2025); Schwartz and Ungar (2015)).

### The usefulness of creating lexicons: interpretability, content validity, integration with deep learning, and benchmarking LLMs

Creating new lexicons can complement deep learning approaches and other lexicons in a variety of ways. First, there is often a need for interpretable models. Lexicons enable interpretable models in the following manner: if a lexicon contains multiple constructs (e.g., fighting, family, empathy), then by counting tokens of a lexicon’s constructs in documents, we can achieve interpretable variables that can be used in a model that predicts a given target variable. That is, a model can learn to weigh the counts of each construct accordingly to optimize prediction. Then, feature importance analysis can convey which features are most important for prediction, which is not directly retrievable from decoder LLMs. If the model is an interpretable one (e.g., linear regression, decision tree), then one can explain exactly how input data was assigned a given output. This is useful for improving trust in the model and to advance the scientific understanding of how the features are related to the target variable. Deep learning models are considered black boxes because we cannot easily and precisely explain the process by which a given input is assigned a specific output (Roscher, Bohn, Duarte, & Garcke, 2020a). While generative LLMs can provide explanations of why they generated a certain result, these may or may not be true (Agarwal, Tanneru, & Lakkaraju, 2024); furthermore, more mechanistic interpretability methods for LLMs are also being developed (Lieberum et al., 2024; Lindsey et al., 2025). LLMs can have bias and make mistakes (Mehrabi, Morstatter, Saxena, Lerman, & Galstyan, 2021). LLMs are increasingly being used for health, criminal justice, and other high-stakes scenarios where not detecting specific phrases as high risk (e.g. “he hit me”, “I just want to escape this pain”) could be particularly problematic (for an example of an edge case in which a deep learning model presumably makes a mistake, see Sup. Mat. Fig. A.1). In the context of suicide risk detection specifically, concerning bias types include underdetection of risk expressions from underrepresented groups whose language patterns are less represented in LLM training data, and overdetection in documents that discuss suicide in educational, journalistic, or research contexts.

When a deep learning model outputs a risk score, it is not possible to know with certainty whether all clinically relevant tokens were detected or whether the model’s prediction relied primarily on the most frequent patterns in its training data. We expect state-of-the-art LLMs to detect most relevant expressions, but this cannot be guaranteed or verified without additional testing. In contrast, a lexicon guarantees exact matches: if a document contains a token in the lexicon, it will be flagged in a deterministic way, and if it does not, it will not. This determinism is particularly valuable in high-stakes scenarios such as suicide risk detection, where missing a specific expression (e.g., a mention of a lethal means or a direct statement of suicidal intent) could have serious consequences. At the same time, lexicons might overdetect (e.g., “I have never felt suicidal” could still match a suicidal construct) and have all the aforementioned limitations (although negated terms can be skipped). Therefore, a strategy might be running both baseline lexicons in parallel to LLMs. If a baseline model is interpretable and is relatively close in performance to a black-box model, then it might be preferred. Not including an interpretable model as a baseline is a lost opportunity to understand more about how variables are associated with the target variable for scientific inquiry (Roscher, Bohn, Duarte, & Garcke, 2020b).

A second reason to create new lexicons is being able to measure what we actually want to measure in text; instead, we often measure whatever existing tools offer. Measuring constructs relevant to our target measurement (e.g., dozens of important risk factors for suicide; most prototypical expression of eating disorder symptoms to detect eating disorders) increases content validity, the degree to which a measurement tool covers a representative sample of the behavior to be measured (see (Anastasi & Urbina, 1997) p. 114). If the goal is to, for instance, understand how individuals with and without suicidal thoughts differ in their mentions of different constructs, then using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) is insufficient, as it is a lexicon with very few constructs directly related to mental illness (Boyd, Ashokkumar, Seraj, & Pennebaker, 2022b). Similarly, a pre-trained sentiment analysis model, which only provides positive, negative, and neutral labels, would lack content validity for clinical mental health constructs. One alternative to using an existing tool that does not capture the construct of interest is to measure it by training a new deep learning model (e.g., (Zuromski et al., 2024)). However, researchers may not be able to obtain enough labeled data or technical expertise to train or fine-tune the model. If they do, it is still common that they would only be able to find enough samples to label just a few constructs across documents instead of the many constructs they might want to measure. Nevertheless, lexicon’s limitations (e.g., word sense ambiguity, binary inclusion) can lead to false positives and false negatives which may decrease the content validity for a given construct. LLMs provide a new alternative for text classification that has all the advantages of standard supervised deep learning (e.g., data-driven, potentially learning contextual and long-term dependencies) and can often generate good results zero-shot, without any additional training data (Amin, Mao, Cambria, & Schuller, 2023; Gretz et al., 2023). However, many datasets are sensitive and cannot be submitted to a generative AI Application Programming Interface (API) of the large online only models. Open-source generative AI models (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Gemma) are becoming a promising alternative, generally require GPU capabilities for performance, and technical expertise to execute locally and programmatically. Smaller language models (e.g., Microsoft Phi, encoder LLMs such as DistilBERT) can often be run without a GPU on a standard laptop for moderately sized datasets, and user-friendly interfaces in R and Python have reduced the technical barrier considerably. However, they tend to have lower performance than frontier models (GPT, Gemini, Claude). Therefore, a well-validated lexicon might be able to capture the tokens that were included. Building a lexicon is something domain experts without deep learning expertise can do, and we offer tools to automate this process.

A third reason lexicons are useful is that they can be combined with deep learning. One example is construct-text similarity (i.e., zero-shot text classification with embeddings) where the cosine similarity between a construct’s lexicon and tokens in the document are computed; then this score is taken as a prediction which can be validated with regard to a ground truth, which enables a more interpretable model (D. M. Low et al., 2025). Lexicons can also be used to find related documents as candidates for training samples, which are later manually annotated (Zuromski et al., 2024). This heuristic is even used as the final label in weak supervision frameworks (Lison, Barnes, & Hubin, 2021).

Finally, lexicons can be used to evaluate and benchmark LLMs in multiple ways including testing content validity, prototypicality, and safety. One use case is if an LLM supposedly detects a given construct (e.g., eating disorders), one should evaluate how accurately does the LLM predict expert-defined lexicon of a construct (e.g., “anorexia”, “bulimia”, “not eating enough”). This would be a content validity test set because it contains a broad set of obvious, prototypical expressions of the construct and therefore should be detected easily than a random test set, which in contrast may prioritize certain expressions (e.g., bulimia) over others (e.g., anorexia) (D. M. Low et al., 2025). Clinically, it would be desirable for an LLM used for screening symptoms to detect a broad array of expressions and not miss certain symptoms for a given target assessment. The lexicon can be used as a content validity test set as is, or its tokens can be used to generate sentences. In the clinical domain, this cannot be done by using a list of symptoms from a diagnostic manual given there are many ways of describing each symptom in colloquial language, which a lexicon could contain. Another use case is analyzing the generated text of an LLM: do chatbots generate the scope of tokens available in an expert-validated lexicon? A third use case is analyzing dialogue: how prototypical of a given construct are the expressions of one of the speakers? Are they mentioning key symptoms (e.g., anorexia) or tangential ones (“I haven’t been having much of an appetite lately”). By having a lexicon with prototypicality ratings by experts, this could be answered. This can be used clinically to understand symptom awareness (i.e., using clear symptom names rather than indirect descriptions), willingness to disclosure symptoms, and symptom phenomenology. Regarding AI Safety, we can use keywords to flag conversations where potentially harmful content is mentioned (e.g., exploitation, hate speech, suicide methods and encouragement, criminal methods). A generative AI model could be trained to identify these expressions (Inan et al., 2023), but who determines which tokens are most problematic? Having ratings of tokens by experts would be beneficial.

### Prior work on creating lexicons manually and automatically

Many lexicons exist, including the General Inquirer (Stone, Dunphy, Smith, & Ogilvie, 1962), SEANCE (Crossley, Kyle, & McNamara, 2017), DLATK (Schwartz et al., 2017), and LIWC (Boyd et al., 2022a). LIWC is has been widely used in psychology research and other domains. It attempts to cover a broad domain of constructs (e.g., death, family, body) and many linguistic properties (e.g., word count, types of pronouns). It has been used for detecting mental health conditions including suicide risk (Sert & Ülker, 2023; Yan, Li, Liu, Li, & Yu, 2024). Some of its main limitations are: (1) it is not free to use and is closed source; (2) it is limited to a small set of categories that may not capture most constructs of interest for a given study. In our study, we will focus on measuring suicidal thoughts and behaviors: in this context, LIWC is missing many mental illness related constructs (e.g., self-injury, trauma, eating/body image crises) and therefore lacks content validity for most mental health conditions; (3) some categories have only a few tokens and others having questionable exclusions (Crossley et al., 2017); and (4) some constructs are very broad: while LIWC does not provide the final list of each category for proprietary reasons, one can find what were the matches in a given dataset for each category (although some categories remain closed-source). For instance, the Physical category includes “gut”, “vodka”, “gay”, “suicide”, “therapeutic”, and “live”. If a study finds an association between this category and some variable of interest, it is not clear what exactly is being measured given how heterogeneous it is.

Methods for creating lexicons have largely been manual, such as having judges manually add them (Boyd et al., 2022a; Shapira et al., 2021), crowdsourcing (Mohammad & Turney, 2013), and translation from lexicons in other languages (Shapira et al., 2021). Automated methods include word embedding similarity (Fast, Chen, & Bernstein, 2016), WordNet synonyms (Fellbaum, 2010), word scores, which find the words that are more likely in one set of documents versus another through extensions of odds ratio analyses (Monroe, Colaresi, & Quinn, 2008); therefore, words that characterize a set of construct-specific documents can form a lexicon for that construct. But this requires a labeled dataset, a control group of documents (and each control group may change the final word scores), and as with word co-occurrences it results in some words that characterize each group in a specific dataset but may also not be prototypical overall.

### Choosing prototypical tokens when building a lexicon

Lexicons are made up of multiple constructs, each one with a set of relevant tokens. How should we judge whether certain tokens should belong in a construct’s lexicon? Constructs are properties often considered to be constructed or defined by human experts and therefore are theoretical (Markus & Borsboom, 2013). Here we use construct as an umbrella term encompassing risk factors (empirically identified predictors of an outcome, such as hopelessness predicting suicide), symptoms (observable or self-reported indicators of a clinical condition, such as depressed mood), and behaviors (observable actions, such as self-injury).

When selecting tokens for a lexicon construct, we follow Rosch’s Prototype Theory (Rosch, 1973) in preferring tokens that are prototypical of a construct —that is, the most typical examples that come to mind when thinking of the category— rather than tokens that are merely semantically related. Including related but non-prototypical tokens risks jeopardizing specificity: for instance, including ’depression’ as a token for Burdensomeness would flag documents about depression that contain no expression of burdensomeness.

Constructs are often latent or not-directly-observable variables that can have different definitions according to different experts and theories. Therefore, for validation it is important to include definitions, so judges can evaluate the inclusion and exclusion of tokens with regard to a specific sense of the construct’s meaning (for further discussion, see Sup. Mat. section B).

### Use case: detecting suicide risk from language

Franklin et al. (2017) show that studies have analyzed similar risk factors for suicide over the last 50 years and suggest there is a need to study new risk factors and study them in novel ways beyond traditional rating-scale questionnaires, which language data provide. Moreover, risk factors may change or be redefined over time, and new lexicons can help measure the new risk factor. Another limitation of prior work is the tendency to study risk factors in bivariate association odds ratio models instead of multivariable and multivariate machine learning models: bivariate associations may increase or decrease when controlling for other variables (Franklin et al., 2017), which is more common in natural language processing (NLP).

Many studies have been carried out predicting suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) from multivariable features extracted from an individual’s written or transcribed text (Goharian et al., 2021; Zuromski et al., 2024) (for reviews, see (Homan et al., 2022; Ophir, Tikochinski, Brunstein Klomek, & Reichart, 2022). In a previous study we have shown that the presence of lexicons and unigrams related to death, money, sadness, and friends help classify suicidal social-media Reddit posts from other non-suicidal mental health posts with an F1 score of 0.85 (D. Low et al., 2020). Another study built a Hebrew lexicon for 11 risk factors for suicidal ideation to assess risk in crisis hotlines’ sessions, and computed the log odds in a logistic regression model and showed Hopelessness, History of suicide attempt, and Deliberate Self-Harm indicated the highest risk (Grimland et al., 2024).

An advantage of measuring not only suicidal constructs, but also risk factors for STBs is that most individuals who die by suicide do not express suicidal intent (Schuck, Calati, Barzilay, Bloch-Elkouby, & Galynker, 2019) but may express other risk factors such as hopelessness, depression, or loneliness. Furthermore, suicidal crises can last for just minutes or hours (Coppersmith et al., 2023; Kleiman et al., 2017), and therefore measuring only expressions of suicidality in language may not capture individuals who are not acutely suicidal but show other warning signs.

Driven by this use-case and the broader question on creating and using lexicons alongside LLMs, our goals are to: Provide a systematic framework and Python package for building lexicons using automated methods such as generative AI.Build a new lexicon to train models that guarantee an exact match, are interpretable, and have high content validity. We choose a high-stakes domain where these properties are particularly useful by building a Suicide Risk Lexicon (SRL) that covers the main risk factors known to be associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors.Demonstrate the SRL’s performance detecting counselor-rated imminent suicide risk relative to an existing and widely-used lexicon LIWC (interpretable, low content validity for suicide risk detection) and to more state-of-the-art approaches using deep learning models (black box and unknown content validity).Compute the feature importance of the Suicide Risk Lexicon to help inform theory as to which constructs are most associated with suicide risk as expressed in everyday natural language.

Regarding expected performance, we expect the SRL, a lexicon covering constructs actually related to the construct we want to measure, to perform better. Deep learning tends to outperform lexicons (Biggiogera et al., 2021), but this may be because the lexicons that were tested such as LIWC tend to lack content validity and specificity for the target construct. Deep learning models can cover a broader range of semantic concepts and learn to weigh these concepts as well as morphosemantic nuances (hedges, degree modifiers, doubt) in order to optimize performance. For these reasons, we expect deep learning model to outperform the SRL; however, provided that the performance of SRL is comparable to the highest performing deep learning model, SRL may be preferred in high-stakes scenarios as it is an interpretable model and has the content validity to reveal how different risk factors contribute to risk, which is useful to advance scientific inquiry.

When we rank feature importance with SRL in predicting suicide risk, we expect the most important features to be those associated with risk of suicide plan or attempt among individuals with suicidal ideation, which we believe will include (measured as the following constructs): suicidal thoughts and behaviors1 (Active Suicidal Ideation & Suicidal Planning, Lethal Means for Suicide, Direct Self-Injury, Passive Suicidal Ideation, Hospitalization, Other Suicidal Language), severe anxiety (Trauma & PTSD), personality disorders (Borderline Personality Disorder), substance use disorders (Other Substance Use), anger (Aggression & Irritability), and Impulsivity; which generally reflects the notion that certain high-arousal negative constructs in suicidal individuals are more associated with more imminent severity and suicidal planning than typical low-arousal constructs such as depressed mood and hopelessness, which in turn may be more associated with only increased risk for suicidal ideation (Franklin et al., 2017; Nock, Hwang, Sampson, & Kessler, 2010). In the same vein, Active Suicidal Ideation & Suicidal Planning and Lethal Means for Suicide we expect will be more important for predicting imminent risk than Passive Suicidal Ideation (Wastler et al., 2023).

## Methods

### Dataset

Crisis Text Line is a nonprofit organization that provides free, 24/7, confidential mental health support for individuals in crisis who can begin a conversation with a trained, volunteer counselor via text messaging or webchat. To validate whether the constructs we measure in text can predict human assessments about the constructs, we built a dataset from Crisis Text Line data, containing 96,723 de-identified crisis counseling conversations between individuals in crisis and counselors from the years 2017 to 2022. Years 2020 and 2021 were omitted to avoid symptoms and concerns related to the Covid-19 pandemic. Demographic data are available for approximately 22% of texters that complete an optional post-session survey, which has been characterized as follows: predominantly young (76% under 25 years old), female (79%), white (53%) and heterosexual (52%) (Pisani et al., 2022). During conversations, counselors assess for suicidal thoughts. If suicidal thoughts are present, they assess for plans (identified means); if plans are present, they assess for access to means (capability); and if access is present, they assess for an imminent (48-hour) timeframe. If a texter is considered to be high risk by the crisis counselor, they will involve a supervisor. The supervisor assesses whether the texter is in immediate danger and unable to create a safety plan. If that is the case, the supervisor may take the necessary steps to contact local emergency services.

We created three groups following these severity levels: imminent risk (conversations that were labeled as having a 48-hour timeframe for planned suicide, imminent risk, and/or an emergency service intervention), suicidal (where the former were not present but any form of suicidal thoughts and behaviors were), and non-suicidal (where other types of crises were present). The sample size was split into training (90%), validation (5%), and test (5%) sets. Within the training set, we balanced the three levels by downsampling non-suicidal and suicidal cases to the imminent sample size to avoid the model over-predicting values closer to the majority value (i.e., non-suicidal) and left the validation and test sets at the natural prevalence rate (non-suicidal: 80%, suicidal: 18%, imminent risk: 2%), resulting in a sample size of 16,360 (i.e., after removing approximately 30% of the data, two years out of the original six years of data, and downsampling the majority classes in the training set). No samples from the validation or test set were used for training or building the lexicon. Seven samples were removed for not having text. The resulting distributions are shown in Sup. Mat., Table C.1. We use only texters’ messages to avoid capturing tokens present in counselor’s questions that are answered negatively (e.g., Counselor: “Are you suicidal?”, texter: “No”, assuming sufficient similar language will be used by the texter).

This study involves secondary analysis of de-identified data provided by Crisis Text Line under a data sharing agreement without access to information that would link IDs to texters, which does not meet the definition of Human Subjects research of our institution, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Therefore it is exempt from Institutional Review Board (IRB) review. Texters who contact Crisis Text Line agree to its terms of service prior to initiating a conversation. Crisis Text Line’s privacy policy permits the use and sharing of anonymized data with qualified researchers to inform public health.

### Protocol for building and validating a lexicon

Building off of other lexicon construction and validation procedures (Boyd et al., 2022a; Shapira et al., 2021), we went through a series of steps to build the Suicide Risk Lexicon, which we expect will be similar for building lexicons in other domains beyond mental health. To support lexicon construction, we are releasing a Python package construct-tracker (D. M. Low, 2024) 2 and tutorial 3 to build lexicons and apply them with more ease and improve reproducibility.

Next we describe the choices we took for our use case, although many of these choices are customizable. Additional considerations are provided in Sup. Mat. C.2, section “Protocol for building and validating a lexicon.”

#### Step 1. Choose constructs and seed examples

Once a target variable to be measured is defined (e.g., imminent suicide risk in our case), relevant associated constructs should be obtained. We compiled a list of risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors (either suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, or suicide death) from reviews and meta-analyses (Bentley et al., 2016; Franklin et al., 2017; Glenn et al., 2018; Nock, 2010; Schuck et al., 2019; Silverman, Berman, Sanddal, O’carroll, & Joiner Jr, 2007; Turecki et al., 2019). Risk factors were extracted by one author (DML) by compiling any factor identified in this literature as a predictor of suicidal ideation, attempt, or death in at least one meta-analysis. Then prototypical seed examples were added to guide automated lexicon generation.

#### Step 2. Automatically create a preliminary lexicon with generative AI

Generative AI models take in a prompt or instruction and generate a response in natural language. These models can be called from different APIs (e.g., OpenAI, OpenRouter, Azure, HuggingFace). construct-tracker (D. M. Low, 2024) is built on top of the litellm package v1.26.0 which can make API requests to hundreds of models. We chose GPT-4 Turbo (gpt-4–1106-preview), OpenAI’s follow-up to GPT-4, as it was first on the Chatbot Arena LMSYS leaderboard (Chiang et al., 2024) when we created the lexicon. After testing multiple prompts (i.e., prompt engineering), we found one that consistently returned prototypical tokens (variables and an example are displayed in angle brackets): “Provide many single words and some short phrases related to <social withdrawal> (in the <mental health> domain). Each token should be separated by a semicolon. Do not return duplicate tokens. Do not provide any explanation or additional text beyond the tokens. Here are some examples (include these in the list): <wish to be alone; don’t want to see anyone; want people to leave me alone>.” All prompts included seed examples to guide the type and format of the tokens generated. Prompt engineering involved iteratively varying the wording of the instruction and manually inspecting the generated token lists across three temperature settings (0, 0.5, and 1) to identify the prompt that most consistently returned prototypical, non-redundant tokens in the desired format.

#### Step 3. Add tokens from word score analysis and questionnaires and remove irrelevant tokens

We supplemented the GPT-4 Turbo-generated tokens by adding characteristic words identified through word score analysis (Monroe et al., 2008) on Reddit mental health posts (D. Low et al., 2020) and Crisis Text Line training data, as well as from thesauri and questionnaire items. We then edited tokens to find the shortest form that maximizes true positive matches while minimizing false positives (e.g., preferring “threat” over “threatening”), and removed tokens that were semantically related but not prototypical or prone to false positives due to polysemy (e.g., “blue” for Depressed Mood, “apart” for Loneliness & Isolation). These steps were carried out by one author (DML); domain experts later validated the final token set. See Sup. Mat. C.2.3 for full details and examples.

#### Step 4. Count lexicon tokens in a corpus

Our package construct-tracker counts how many times tokens of a given construct appear in a document. Tokens were lemmatized using Spacy v3.6.1 to capture morphological variants, exact matching was enforced for tokens of four letters or fewer to avoid spurious substring matches, and counts were normalized by document word count (Boyd et al., 2022b). See Sup. Mat. C.2.4 for further details.

#### Step 5. Calibrate lexicon by finding false positive and false negatives

A critical step is verifying whether a token for a given construct (e.g., “race” for the Discrimination construct) is matching a token within a context that is unrelated (e.g., “my thoughts race”), which would be a false positive. We calibrated the lexicon through several substeps (see Sup. Mat. C.2.5 for full details): (1) comparing token match rates in 10k mental health versus 10k non-mental health Reddit posts using log odds ratios (Monroe et al., 2008) to identify and remove tokens more characteristic of non-mental health text (e.g., “blue” from Depressed Mood, “unfair” from Discrimination); (2) reviewing matched tokens in the Crisis Text Line training set in context to remove false positives (e.g., “give up” for Passive Suicidal Ideation) and add missed tokens; (3) inspecting 20 random r/SuicideWatch documents for false negatives; and (4) removing tokens unmatched in either the Crisis Text Line training set or r/SuicideWatch posts (D. Low et al., 2021), retaining 60.2

#### Step 6. Validate with domain expert judgments

One licensed clinical psychologist and two trainees (coauthors KHB, OR, and DC) with 6–12 years of experience in suicide research and suicide risk assessment provided independent judgements on the degree to which each token is a prototypical expression of a given construct. See Sup. Mat. section C.2.6 for full instructions. When doing so, we also ask judges to consider how prevalent the potential alternative senses of a token are that are unrelated to the construct at hand, because this would lead to a different amount of expected false positives (flagging a document not about the construct) and false negatives (missing a document about the construct). “Depression” is more commonly used for mental health than economy or geology; whereas “alarm” would likely create many false positives for Panic (“The report alarmed us”, “The alarm went off”). To ease validation, each construct’s list is ordered by similarity to average embedding across seed examples using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings (Face & Transformers, 2024). Given our use-case, these clinicians were asked to decide to what degree they would want to flag a document for a given construct (Direct Self-Injury) if it contained a given token (“hurt myself”). Response options were 0 No (or it might create too many false positives), 1 (More no than yes), (More yes than no), 4 Definitely prototypical (or I would definitely want to flag it).

#### Step 7. Estimate inter-rater reliability

All tokens for suicidal constructs (given their centrality to the study’s aims) were rated by all three clinicians. Tokens for the remaining constructs were rated by two raters. We computed the intra-class correlation coefficient using the R irr package (Gamer, 2010) on clinician’s judgements when tokens had three ratings. Inter-rater agreement (proportion of equal rating) was performed for tokens with two raters. Common cutoffs for inter-rater agreement are poor for values less than .40, fair for values between .40 and .59, good for values between .60 and .74, and excellent for values between .75 and 1.0 (Cicchetti, 1994). We expect many tokens to be 3/3 prototypicality given the pre-curation efforts; in these scenarios of high agreement, other common metrics such as Cohen’s kappa suffer from the Kappa paradox and return very low values (Derksen, Bruinsma, Goslings, & Schep, 2024).

### Lexicon validation: predicting suicide risk score with machine learning

We compared the following feature vectors’ ability to detect perceived suicide risk (as described in the Dataset section with possible values 1, 2, or 3) from Crisis Text Line by training them using Ridge regression (a linear model) using sklearn v1.2.0 and light gradient-boosting machine (LGBMRegressor) from the lightgbm package v4.3.0. We compared these to deep learning models, which serve black-box upper bounds to the lexicon-based interpretable models. See Sup. Mat. C.3 for details on hyperparameter tuning using Bayesian optimization and GPU specifications.

#### Suicide Risk Lexicon:

we report performance using just the tokens automatically generated by GPT-4 Turbo as described in step 2 (SRL GPT-4), the unvalidated model following steps 1–5 (SRL GPT-4 + manual), and the model with the lexicon validated by clinicians (SRL GPT-4 + manual + clinicians). Counts are normalized.

#### LIWC-22:

LIWC includes semantic constructs (family, anger) and nonsemantic linguistic features (pronoun, unique words). To compare this to our lexicon of semantic constructs, we report results with only semantic features (LIWC-22 semantic) and all features (LIWC-22).

#### all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (deep learning, not fine-tuned):

we encode documents with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 deep learning embeddings (Face & Transformers, 2024) and change the maximum token length to 500. These embeddings are optimized for semantic similarity of paraphrases and offer a good balance between performance on a semantic textual similarity task and a fast inference time. This offers a deep learning baseline that provides researchers an easier-to-implement alternative to the fine-tuned deep neural networks we use.

#### DistilBERT (deep learning, fine-tuned):

distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased pre-trained model was fine-tuned through the transformers package (Wolf et al., 2020) on the training set to adjust the embedding space to the datasets language style. Distilbert was chosen as a faster-training alternative to potentially more powerful models (e.g., MPNet); distillation reduces the size of BERT by 40%, while retaining 97% of its capabilities and being 60% faster (Sanh et al., 2021).

#### MPNet (deep learning, fine-tuned):

microsoft/mpnet-base pretrained model was fine-tuned in a similar manner on a single NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPU with 25 GB memory. MPNet was chosen because of its superior performance to BERT, RoBERTa, and XNET on multiple tasks (Song, Tan, Qin, Lu, & Liu, 2020).

#### Performance evaluation.

Given the test set is skewed, standard metrics such as root mean squared error (RMSE) will be heavily influenced by the majority value (i.e., 1 or nonsuicidal); therefore, we focus on macro average RMSE which takes the average of the RMSE computed on each value following recommendation in (Baccianella, Esuli, & Sebastiani, 2009) and Spearman rho between true and predicted values to assess the degree to which models are able to increase predicted scores as true severity increases.

For all statistical tests reported in this study, we use a significance threshold of = .05.

### Feature importance analysis to inform theory

Understanding which variables are associated with suicide risk from a language perspective can help inform theory of suicide risk. For Ridge models we compute the absolute standardized coefficients. For LGBMRegressor models we calculated the improvement in the information gain (i.e., the splitting criterion) from using a given feature in a tree’s split (i.e., how much a given feature helps to reduce the error).

## Results

### Suicide Risk Lexicon

See Fig. 1 for the Suicide Risk Lexicon shown through a custom circular network done via the networkx package (Hagberg, Swart, & S Chult, 2008). The edges represent the similarity between average embeddings of the seed examples. Some constructs across theoretical categories are very similar due to similar tokens (e.g., “dad died” in Grief & Bereavement and “dad” in Relationship & kinship) or the same tokens (“overdose” in Lethal Means for Suicide and in Other Substance Use). Definitions of each construct are in Sup. Mat., Table D.1.

The seed examples, amount of tokens per construct, and top matches are shown in Table 1 for suicidal constructs. Examples for all constructs can be found in Sup. Mat. Table D.2 along with the proportion of final tokens generated by GPT-4 Turbo, the word score analyses, and manually added tokens. The median [minimum and maximum] tokens across constructs is 59 [22–173].

In Sup. Mat. Fig. D.1 we display the amount of matches across datasets. Active Suicidal Ideation, Lethal means for suicide, Other Suicidal Language, and Other Substance Use have more matches for Imminent Risk than for Suicidal.

### Inter-rater reliability

All tokens from the suicidal constructs were rated by three clinicians for which the ICC (SD) was 0.48 (0.20). IRR was computed at the token level. The inter-rater absolute agreement for remaining constructs was 0.54 (0.18). These would be considered fair according to a common criteria (Cicchetti, 1994). Our procedure resulted in many tokens raters deemed 3/3 prototypical, as expected, due to the pre-curation efforts.

### Predicting suicide risk score with machine learning

In Table 2 we show performance predicting counselor’s assessment of suicide risk. Manually editing and removing tokens from the GPT-4 Turbo lexicon plus adding tokens from other sources (word scores, thesauri) improves prediction as expected and ends up being on par with the all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a pre-trained deep learning embeddings. After following the expert clinician ratings, performance improved, likely because the content validity increased after removing nonprototypical tokens. DistilBERT and MPNet are fine-tuned on the training set and achieve higher performance as expected. MPNet achieves a larger Spearman rho, indicating better prediction of severity increases. Results using ridge regression, consistently worse for all models except all-MiniLM-L6-v2, are shown in Sup. Mat., Table D.3. To understand relative model performance under data scarcity, which is common in clinical research, we trained models using a random subselection of 150 samples from the training set and the SRL-based models were the best performing models (see Sup. Mat., Table D.4).

To compare model performance, we used a paired bootstrap procedure (10,000 iterations; Demšar (2006)). On each iteration, the same set of indices (sampled with replacement from the test-set) was applied to all models, and Spearman’s ρ were computed for each. Pairwise differences (Model A - Model B) were recorded across all iterations, yielding an empirical null distribution for each metric. A 95% percentile confidence interval (CI) was constructed from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of this distribution; a difference was considered statistically significant when the CI excluded zero. All comparisons of Spearman’s ρ > 0.02 were significant (see Sup. Mat. Fig. D.3). The curated Suicide Risk Lexicon significantly outperformed LIWC –albeit by a modest effect size– and MPNet outperformed lexicons. In Sup. Mat., Fig. D.2, we show the scatter plots of true vs. predicted values from LIWC-22 semantic (given similar performance to LIWC-22 with fewer features), SRL GPT-4 + manual + clinicians, and MPNet (which had the highest Spearman rho’s).

### Feature importance analysis to inform theory

In Table 3, we rank how important each feature is for predicting suicide risk using the SRL and LIWC with semantic features to compare only semantic features. Regarding our hypotheses, suicidal constructs, Other Subtance Use, Borderline Personality Disorder, and Trauma & PTSD were more important for prediction than Depressed Mood and Hopelessness. Also, as hypothesized, Active Suicidal Ideation and Lethal means for Suicide were more important than Passive Suicidal Ideation. Contrary to our hypotheses, Depressed Mood was more important than Hospitalization and Aggression & Irritability.

## Discussion

The Suicide Risk Lexicon (SRL) models outperformed an existing widely-used lexicon LIWC –albeit modestly–, which is expected given LIWC does not have content validity for suicide risk detection, and many of its categories are too broad or heterogeneous to be specific to mental illness. Surprisingly, a fully automated GPT-4 Turbo-derived lexicon, without the manual curation or clinician ratings, is able to achieve relatively good performance. The advantage of using a new lexicon is not just interpretability but also content validity: measuring a representative sample of constructs associated with the target measurement, which allows us to discuss theory. Once validated, reusing the same lexicon across studies is in fact desirable for cumulative science, enabling comparability of findings across datasets and contexts. The SRL is released openly for exactly this purpose. SOTA LLMs also provide this capability, but are not preferred or used by many researchers. We also add to theoretical debates on suicide risk factors by providing a complementary view of them from a natural language perspective in a new domain, crisis counseling, where the main data type is text. We partially confirm what rating-scale assessments have found with regard to risk for suicidal planning (Nock et al., 2010; Wastler et al., 2023): mention of Lethal Means for Suicide, Active suicidal ideation & Suicidal Planning (thoughts and plans about killing oneself), Other Suicidal Language, Direct Self-Injury, Other substance use were the most important features for prediction. All of these were more important than Passive Suicidal Ideation, Depressed Mood, and Hopelessness, as expected. Contrary to our hypotheses, Hospitalization and Aggression & Irritability were less important for prediction than Depressed Mood, and Impulsivity was not important for prediction. It is important to note that these results pertain to the prediction of counselor-rated suicide risk —a clinical judgment made during a crisis counseling session— rather than directly observed behaviors such as suicide attempts or deaths. The rank of feature importance may differ when predicting behavioral outcomes prospectively.

Our hypotheses are based on reviews and meta-analyses whose findings are derived from samples assessed for suicide planning or suicide attempts through rating scales, often prospectively, whereas our sample seems to have confirmed suicide planning and imminent risk (with perceived suicidal desire, intent, and capability) at the highest severity level, with only some cases being actual suicide attempts. It is possible the ways in which symptoms are expressed in natural language reveal risk factors differently than rating scales, and therefore findings from natural language provide a different window into understanding the factors that predict a given assessment. The same sample of individuals answering rating-scale questionnaires may return a different rank of risk factors. Rating scales have the advantage of probing specific constructs in a specific way, while natural language in this study has the advantage of being able to express many more risk factors than an individual questionnaire (whatever the individual expresses and is asked about in the conversation), captured ecologically at the very moment a person is perceived to have imminent risk.

### Content validity: an interpretable model needs an interpretable theory

Even if we use features that are interpretable, it still may be difficult to interpret why a feature is associated with the dependent variable. “Physical” and “clout” were among the top features for the LIWC model (see Table 3). It is possible to come up with post-hoc explanations of these associations and for most LIWC features, we can explore matches in our dataset: Physical contains many words including “suicide”, “kill”, “die.” However, it also contains many unrelated words to suicide such as “spice” and “cbd”, and therefore lacks specificity for suicide. Clout (i.e., expression of power) is kept proprietary and also appears unspecific to our use-case. These types of interpretable, but semantically unrelated models lack content validity for suicide risk. They would also lack face validity if they subjectively would not seem to be measuring what they claim to measure to the recipients of the model’s assessment (i.e., texters in crisis): we discovered LIWC category Death helps predict suicide risk –which has also shown to predict that a Reddit post is from r/SuicideWatch versus other mental health subreddits (D. Low et al., 2020)– because it contains tokens such as “suicide.” This is intuitive; however, Death is related to Suicide but also to many other domains. We are left wondering whether the LIWC model actually measures suicidality and how this trained model might distinguish documents about Suicidal Ideation versus documents about Ecology that describe animal deaths and killings: Death would likely no longer be an important feature in that classifier. This means the model likely lacks specificity beyond this dataset. The same argument can be made when using feature derived from pre-trained deep learning models (e.g., sentiment, emotions). In contrast, SRL models measure theory-driven variables that are specific to suicide and mental illness. The specificity and direct connections afforded by SRL is thus able to add to the literature on suicide risk factors.

### Limitations

Several limitations should be noted. First, as outlined in the introduction, lexicons are insensitive to contextual information such as hedging and modality. In suicide risk detection, this insensitivity has practical consequences: a document containing “I sort of feel sad” and one containing “I can’t help feeling sad” would receive identical lexicon scores for Depressed Mood, despite the latter expressing a more entrenched and potentially higher-risk affective state. This can introduce systematic bias rather than random error since individuals who express distress through hedged or minimizing language (e.g., “I sort of feel sad”) may systematically receive inflated risk scores despite lower actual severity. Nevertheless, we included constructs of different severity (e.g., passive vs. active suicidal ideation; anxiety vs. panic) to partially address this. Users of the SRL should be aware of this and consider pairing lexicon-based detection with LLMs and with downstream human review in applied settings. We do not think we can improve lexicons to surpass LLM capabilities; they simply serve a different purpose as an interpretable baseline low-resource model (for a discussion on the upper limits of lexicons, see Sup. Mat. section C.4).

Second, the validity evidence presented here is primarily content validity (i.e., including most risk factors for the goal of suicide risk detection and including prototypical expressions of each risk factor; assessed qualitatively) and concurrent criterion validity (i.e., predicting a ground-truth label): we demonstrate that lexicon-based features can predict counselor-rated suicide risk scores out of sample. These are important but a limited form of validation. We do not provide evidence of discriminant validity, different types of reliability, or validity against clinical assessments or real-world behavioral outcomes such as suicide attempts or deaths (see here for a discussion of some of these properties, D. M. Low et al. (2025)). Our goal was to predict risk severity from counselor-based assessments using NLP to estimate relative text-based risk factors; further evaluation of psychometric properties could help determine whether such as model could be deployed to screen for suicide risk.

Third, the dataset comes from a single platform (Crisis Text Line) with a specific demographic profile. The lexicon was developed and validated in English, within a US-based crisis texting context. It is therefore unclear how well the SRL generalizes to other languages, cultural factors, or platforms such as electronic health records, psychotherapy transcripts, or non-Western crisis services. Cultural factors shape how distress and suicidality are expressed in language (e.g., relative disclosure of mental health symptoms, stigma, metaphoric language, humor, and slang –to name a few– may vary across cultures). Future work should examine cross-cultural and cross-platform validity.

Fourth, the performance differences between models are modest and should be interpreted cautiously. We provide macro average RMSE and Spearman rho to characterize model performance, but further validation across other datasets and psychological domains is needed to establish whether these patterns are robust. Claims about which model performs best should be understood as specific to this dataset and task.

Fifth, the method to automatically create lexicons with generative AI we propose is using seed examples, which may introduce subjectivity since different seed words may lead to different lexicons; however, these are not needed for generation (some constructs had only two), but they seem to help generate tokens in the desired style (i.e., short instead of long phrases) and domain (e.g., mental health).

Sixth, the manual curation steps (Steps 3 and 5) were carried out by one author (DML) and are therefore subjective. It is possible that relevant tokens were removed or that irrelevant tokens were retained. Researchers replicating this protocol for other domains should consider having multiple curators independently complete these steps and computing inter-rater reliability, which we did not do for this phase (but did do for the clinician ratings on the final tokens). Nevertheless, while curation can both improve and bias the model, the completely automated non-curated SRL performed relatively well in terms of prediction. More broadly, we recommend calibrating lexicons on the training set rather than the test set to avoid data leakage, and being attentive to polysemic tokens whose high frequency may dominate construct scores in misleading ways (e.g., ’cut’ in Direct Self-Injury); the construct-tracker package supports transparent logging of all additions and removals with timestamps to aid reproducibility (for more discussion, see Sup. Mat. C.5).

Seventh, inter-rater reliability among clinician ratings was fair (ICC = 0.48 for suicidal constructs; inter-rater agreement = 0.54 for remaining constructs) rather than excellent. While this is not uncommon for nuanced clinical constructs and our pre-curation efforts increased agreement, it indicates some instability in judgments about token prototypicality. Future work should examine whether a higher-agreement lexicon yields meaningfully different predictive performance.

Finally, this study was not preregistered. The hypotheses regarding feature importance were based on a prior epidemiological study (Nock et al., 2010).

### Future directions

The findings from the feature importance analysis have direct implications for clinical practice: they suggest that screening tools and risk assessment protocols for crisis counseling contexts should prioritize active suicidal ideation, lethal means access, and direct self-injury over more distal indicators such as depressed mood and hopelessness, at least when the goal is identifying imminent rather than longer-term risk. Future work should examine whether these findings replicate in other clinical settings —such as emergency departments or outpatient psychotherapy— and whether lexicon-based features can be integrated into real-time clinical decision support tools in a way that is transparent and auditable.

Beyond this application, several extensions of the SRL and the construct-tracker protocol could be pursued. The lexicon could be refined by further subdividing constructs (e.g., separating loneliness from isolation; distinguishing prescribed from non-prescribed substances in Lethal Means), adding protective factors (e.g., Optimism, Social Support, Reasons for Living). Cross-cultural and cross-platform validation is a priority given the demographic specificity of the current dataset. Additional methods such as topic modeling could help discover words and phrases that predict suicide risk in a data-driven way. Finally, lexicons can be combined with deep learning in a variety of ways — including as content validity test sets for LLM benchmarking, as candidate generators for weak supervision, and as probing tools for embedding spaces — that are facilitated by the construct-tracker package and detailed in (D. M. Low et al., 2025).

The criteria for creating and combining constructs is that it is useful enough for detecting suicide risk in text. Certain constructs could be further divided (e.g., loneliness and isolation; subtypes of anxiety symptoms and disorders; lethal means into potentially prescribed medication vs. non-prescribed substance or violent vs. nonviolent. Other risk factors could be added (suppress unwanted thoughts) as well as other protective factors that could be added are Optimism, Resilience, Social Support, Meaning, reasons for living (for further discussion, see Sup. Mat. E.1). We avoided measuring heterogeneous disorders such as major depressive disorder because it is psychometrically futile if the score is the same for individuals with very different symptoms (Fried, Flake, & Robinaugh, 2022). We instead took a symptom-based approach (e.g., measuring Depressed Mood, Hopelessness), but this could be further developed to address even more fine-grained symptoms. Lexicons could be built by having each construct represent a polarity (e.g., happy-sad) to return scores that fall on that polarity (Shapira et al., 2021). Other models and datasets could be compared and we offer a package that leverages most commonly used APIs to do this.

## Conclusions

We demonstrated how LLMs can be leveraged to create large lexicons semi-automatically that cover a wide range of constructs, improving content validity over existing tools like LIWC. Specifically, we developed and validated the open-source Suicide Risk Lexicon (SRL), a domain-specific tool designed to predict suicide risk from text data. By tailoring lexicons to specific domains, we show that lexicons can achieve performance comparable to simple deep learning models, with the added benefit of interpretability —making it easier to understand which variables are associated with the target outcome. We still would prioritize LLMs for text classification, but they remain out of reach for many researchers without AI expertise. Zero-shot prompting of generative AI no-code GUI tools has made some aspects of text classification more accessible to non-programmers than before. The primary advantages of lexicons over LLMs are therefore not accessibility per se, but rather interpretability, determinism, and privacy (no data need be sent to an external API). Lexicons may additionally be used to benchmark LLMs through a content validity test set. We were able to estimate the relative risk of many known suicide risk factors in a novel domain, as is crisis counseling conversations.

Our study provides a systematic protocol and accompanying software package that streamline the process of building domain-specific lexicons that can be used in other fields, enabling researchers and practitioners without deep learning expertise to create interpretable models with high content validity. This approach not only enhances accessibility but also allows for more efficient lexicon development than manual curation, improving both scalability and accuracy in text classification tasks. Our work opens the door for further exploration into the integration of lexicons with machine learning models, as well as using expert-validated lexicons to benchmark LLMs.
